The April 29, 2020 FOMC statement signals maximum accommodation at the zero lower bound, open-ended Treasury and MBS purchases, and robust repo operations amid severe pandemic-driven declines in activity and employment. April 2020 SLOOS evidence intensifies the negative read by documenting broad tightening in bank credit supply across C&I (including middle-market), CRE/multifamily, and consumer products, wider spreads and higher line costs, weaker demand in CRE, and expectations for further tightening—reinforcing impaired credit intermediation despite policy backstops.

Beige Book references add texture consistent with ongoing headwinds: manufacturing was affected by trade-related uncertainty, and consumer-facing sectors such as auto dealers and general retail were key pressure points across Districts. While some Districts cited shortages of skilled labor and wage pressures and noted input-cost influences on prices (freight, metals, tariffs, natural gas, wages) and varied crop price pressures, these pockets of tightness and cost pass-through are too narrow to offset the broader contraction and credit tightening. Netting these insights, the Beige Book marginally reinforces the downside narrative arising from SLOOS and the FOMC’s concern about impaired credit flow, with only limited mitigating signals from isolated labor tightness.
